narrative.text: 23:10. The polls open at seven. The campaign is over by law at midnight; after that, nobody in this building may say anything to anyone about anything that matters. The office is dark except for the desk lamp. Somewhere down the corridor a radio is playing low.
It is playing the Sorvald quartet. Someone downstairs has a sense of humor, or a long memory.
Theron's order to open the Chancellery gates for one hour on Wednesday sits on the blotter, unsigned, waiting for a result.
The order to open the Chancellery gates for one hour on Wednesday sits on the blotter, unsigned, waiting for a result.
The order to open the Chancellery gates for one hour on Wednesday sits on the blotter, unsigned, waiting for a result.
Wednesday in the diary has one entry, as you promised the hall: DESK, 08:00. Nobody has dared add anything to it.
The number of the cemetery office in Kravenstal is written on the blotter in your own hand. You told six hundred people you would call it on Wednesday. You haven't decided what you will say.
In the second drawer, under the Aldenmoor file, is the carbon of a letter dated the Thursday after the vote. You haven't opened the drawer all week.
Krel comes in without knocking and without a folder. He never brings paper to the conversations that matter. He sits, which he has never done in this room.

Thornfeld. Three districts, thirty-eight thousand ballots. The polling says they break for Kolvar sixty-forty. The returning officers in all three are Halvek-era appointments, and the ballot boxes are sealed with wax in the old manner. If a seal is found defective at the count, the box is void. I have men who can be at the count. Nobody would need to touch a ballot. Only the wax.
You'll be interested to know that two of the three returning officers were defence counsel for the BNI men you put on trial in week seventy-two. The system remembers its lawyers.
The twelve men from the telephone exchange never came back, as you know. Their friends are in Thornfeld. They are not waiting for me to act. They are waiting to see whether I do.
You covered for my men once, in week ninety-one. They haven't forgotten. These are the same men. They are, if anything, more careful now.
You arrested three of my men in week ninety-one. The ones who are left are the careful ones. I mention it so that you know I am not offering you the careless ones.
And since the quiet office's files went into the boiler, there will be no record of this conversation either way. That was your decision, not mine.
Everything in this building will be read by whoever wins. I won't write tonight down. I'd suggest you don't either.
No.
Yours.
Vyktor is not here. You know exactly what he'd say: one word, the right one, and then nothing. You find you can't guess which word.
The telephone rings once at 23:20. Dusek, from the General Staff building. 'Barracks. All of them.' She rings off before you can answer.
A note came by hand this afternoon from Colonel Haas of the 4th Rifles: 'We will vote like everyone else. Thank you for the board.' It's on the corner of the desk.
Outside the gate, the 4th Rifles' delegation stands in silence for its hour, as it has every evening this week. They leave at midnight, when the law says they must.
The Kravenstal precinct captains telephoned at nine. The foundry wards are 'too close to call', which, in Kravenstal, means angry but present.

Kolvar's final rally ended at ten in front of the Central District station where he was held. He spoke for eleven minutes and finished with the same sentence he started with: 'Halvek had folders too.'
Kolvar held no rally tonight. His campaign office closed at six. His name is still on every ballot in the country, and the folder is still in your drawer.
Jonas telephones at 23:30. He says one word, the same one you wrote in the diary margin: Thursday. Then he asks whether you have eaten.

Three chalk marks are drawn on the Chancellery steps for tomorrow night. A clerk has gone over them in white paint so the rain will not take them. Liora would say that is the most honest thing in the building.
There is a note from Tomas on the desk, pushed under the blotter. Whatever happens tomorrow, thank you for not promising.
From Aldenmoor, by the evening post, a single line on house paper: The seals are still unbroken. So is the agreement. A.M.
The Aldenmoor gates were empty of leaflets all week. The house says nothing. Silence, from that family, used to cost money. Tonight it is free.
Kolvar's harbor posters went up on house hoardings this morning, paid for in the open. Aleksei, at least, has learned to buy things in daylight.
The thirty-year seal covers what the quiet office has done. It does not cover what it does tonight. I checked the wording.
The forty-one colonels are on duty at the polling stations as reserve marshals. I have their files. You have them too. Neither of us has ever used them.
Number Three furnace is lit tonight in Kravenstal. You can't see it from here. You keep looking north anyway.
Vostane's paper on Number Three furnace is still in her drawer, dated for the Thursday after the vote. You have now postponed two different things to that Thursday.
The morning papers scored the debate on the line where you named what failed. The Voice printed the list. The Herald printed only the word failed.
The morning papers led with your question about 1951. Kolvar has not answered it in nine days. His silence is louder than his rallies.
The morning papers printed your sentence about the Court ruling against you twice and you letting it stand. Some of them printed it as praise.
You put a reprimand in my file in week ninety-one. I've read it. It's well drafted. I'm offering this anyway, which should tell you how close I think tomorrow is.
Some of the officers we stopped in week seventy-two are polling-station marshals tomorrow. Nobody ever told them what we knew. Their loyalty is a coin that hasn't landed yet.
Since you went to war with the oligarchs in week seventy-two, their money has paid for every Kolvar leaflet in Thornfeld. They're doing in daylight what I'm offering to do with wax.

Thirty-eight thousand ballots, and not one would need touching. Only the wax. Father's district voted in 1946 with wax seals like these. He was taken the year after. I've never known whether the two things were connected. I've always assumed they were.

choices.text: "No. Every box is counted. Including the ones that lose me this."
"Only the wax." Nod once, and don't ask which boxes.
Telephone the Forum's observer mission before midnight. Put an international observer at every Thornfeld count, and tell Krel why.
"Your resignation, Matthias. Tonight. And the quiet office closes with you, whoever wins tomorrow."

narrative.text: As you wish. I'll tell them to go home.
He stands and buttons his coat. At the door he stops, the way old men stop at doors in this building, and doesn't turn round.
Kolvar's people won't make you the same offer, Chancellor. They'll just do it. I hope you win by more than thirty-eight thousand.
So do I. I'll never know whether I needed them, and that's the point of refusing. If I win, I won. If I lose, I lost a fair count. Father would have settled for either.

choices.text: Every box counted. The polls open at seven, and I'll sleep, or try to.

narrative.text: Krel nods once in return and leaves. He doesn't say goodnight. He never does when he's working.

At 23:58 you take a sheet of Chancellery paper, write the time on it, and fold it into the back of your diary. You don't know why. Perhaps so that somebody, one day, can know exactly when it happened.
Only the wax. Nobody touches a ballot. I'll win or I'll lose, and either way I'll never know whether I won. Halvek must have had nights like this one. I used to think he slept well.

choices.text: The wax is Krel's problem now. The question of whether I won is mine, forever.

narrative.text: The Forum's mission chief answers on the fourth ring, in a hotel bar in Stellamere. By 02:00 nine observers are on the night train to Thornfeld. By seven, one is standing behind every returning officer in the three districts, watching the wax.
You've told every newspaper in the West that you expected your own election to be rigged. Kolvar will call it an insult to Thornfeld. He'll be right. It's also the only lock I couldn't have picked.

Nine strangers at the count, to stop a man who works for me. If a seal is defective now, it's defective in front of witnesses. Locking my own door from the outside is the strangest thing I've done in office.

choices.text: Nine observers on the night train. Every seal in Thornfeld watched, Krel's included.

narrative.text: He looks at you for a long time. Then he takes a fountain pen from his inside pocket and writes three lines on the back of the visitors' card in his wallet, signs it, and puts it on the desk.
The greenhouse was too exposed, I told you once. So is this office, now. You've made it a room with windows. Someone else will build a room without them. Someone always does.

The quiet office is closed by decree at 23:55, five minutes before the campaign silence would have made it impossible. Its six remaining staff are transferred to the Archive in Ostrava Street with full pensions and orders not to discuss their previous work.

Two years of a second government in the basement, ended on the back of a visiting card. I built it the way Father's enemies built theirs, one necessary night at a time. I don't know if closing it makes me better. It makes me finished with it.

choices.text: Krel's resignation on a visiting card. The quiet office closed five minutes before the silence.
